intro: August Jaeger talks Elgar out of giving up composition by singing him Beethoven. Nimrod remembers that friendship in a string melody that grows until the whole orchestra is singing.

sections.label: A · Violins on the D string
sections.mNote: A quiet E♭-major melody in three beats

sections.label: A′ · The woodwinds join
sections.mNote: Flute and clarinet share the violin phrase

sections.label: A″ · Brass beneath the broad melody
sections.mNote: Legatissimo, with timpani and a fuller bass

sections.label: Coda · The last E♭ chord
sections.mNote: The strings descend and the orchestra falls quiet

cues.title: Violins on one string
cues.text: The first violins sing very softly on the D string. Divided violas and second violins fill the chords beneath them. The Adagio moves in three beats, but the tune stretches across the bar lines in one long breath.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 52, rehearsal 33: Adagio in 3/4, first violins sul D and ppp, divided inner strings and a quiet bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Jaeger, the hunter
cues.text: August Jaeger works for Novello, Elgar’s publisher. He reads the scores closely, praises them, argues with their composer and sometimes demands changes. His surname means hunter in German; Elgar names his variation after the mighty hunter Nimrod in the Book of Genesis.
cues.evidence: Jaeger’s work at Novello, his advice and criticism, and the name’s biblical reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, variation IX. See also John Pickard’s BBC note: https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_enigma.shtml

cues.title: Jaeger sings Beethoven
cues.text: In 1904 Elgar tells Dora Penny how Jaeger talks him out of giving up composition. Jaeger points to Beethoven’s troubles, sings the slow movement of the Pathétique Sonata and insists: “And that is what you must do.” The opening of Nimrod carries a hint of that melody.
cues.evidence: Dora Powell (née Penny), Edward Elgar: Memories of a Variation, second edition (1947), pp. 110–111: Elgar’s 1904 account of Jaeger’s visit and words, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

cues.title: The orchestra sings together
cues.text: Elgar writes legatissimo: the notes joined as closely as possible. Woodwinds double the rising violin tune, brass fill the chords, and timpani support the bass. Even at its fullest, the music keeps the long bow stroke of the opening.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 54–56, rehearsals 35–37: the build into legatissimo at rehearsal 36, with wind, brass and timpani reinforcement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Winds join the strings
transitions.from: A · Violins on the D string
transitions.how: The E♭-major Adagio takes another breath. Flute and clarinet share the violin melody, with bassoons and horns filling the chords below. The cellos divide, and the basses move under the rising phrase. A new crescendo grows from pianissimo; the three-beat pace stays unchanged.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 52–53, rehearsal 34: flute, clarinet, bassoon and horn entries around the string melody, followed by crescendo.

transitions.title: The bass gathers the orchestra
transitions.to: A″ · Brass beneath the broad melody
transitions.how: Quiet oboe and clarinet phrases lead to a rising cello line. Bassoons and horns join the crescendo, then the E♭-major melody opens out at legatissimo. Timpani and double basses anchor it below; trumpets, trombones and tuba fill out the sustained chords.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 54–55, rehearsals 35–36: wind phrases above moving cellos, crescendo molto and the full-orchestra legatissimo.

transitions.title: E♭ major falls quiet
transitions.from: A″ · Brass beneath the broad melody
transitions.how: At the final ritardando, the violin line descends and the orchestra drops from fortissimo to pianissimo. Brass and timpani stop. Clarinets, bassoons and strings hold the last E♭-major chord over a low E♭, with a pause above the final bar.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 56, rehearsal 37 and the final bars: ritardando, diminishing dynamics, wind and brass releases, and the held E♭-major close.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, IX. Nimrod, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 52–56, rehearsal figures 33–37: strings alone, the gathering wind and brass, and the final quiet E♭-major chord.

timeline.note: First violins sing on the D string above divided violas, second violins and a quiet bass.
Flute and clarinet double the rising line; bassoons and horns fill the string harmony.
Oboes join the upper melody while low reeds and horns deepen the supporting chords.
Timpani enter beneath wind chords and the rising string melody.
Trumpets double the melody; trombones and tuba hold chords above the timpani and basses.
Wind and brass chords recede around the descending strings; timpani stop before the final quiet chord.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
